utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. We have a late start due to the technical problems. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Hannis -- Ms. Loukas, I see that you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just want to introduce today to the Court that we have Mr. Andrej Jonovic with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Jonovic. Mr. Hannis, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Witness Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When we begin, Your Honour, may I inform him of why we were delayed, or would Your Honour be willing to do that? I don't know if he's aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic. I first would like to apologise for our late start. It was due to a computer problem, and without that computer we can't review on our screens your testimony; therefore, we had to start late. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Hannis will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Hannis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, when we left off yesterday, we'd been talking about what you described as the organised looting in Bijeljina. I want to move now to the section in your statement that talks about a special police operation to Bijeljina in July 1992. In paragraphs 73 through 77, you describe how you were instructed to go deal with the problems of paramilitaries in Bijeljina. My question to you is: Having been to the Republika Srpska in May and giving training to people, why wasn't the RS able to handle this problem themselves? They had special units of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they didn't want to deal with this themselves, but it was quite obvious that it was a problem that they didn't want to deal with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, to your knowledge, did they have the resources, the manpower, and the equipment, to do what you did?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, they had the manpower. They had the equipment. They had the resources. And they could have dealt with the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement - I'm moving now to paragraph 80 - you describe how the primary paramilitaries that were creating a problem in Bijeljina at that time were Arkan's men and the Red Berets. You told us earlier about when you had first gone to Sarajevo you ran into a group of Red Berets headed by someone named Carli. Were the Red Berets in Bijeljina that same group or a different one?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Berets that I first met in Sarajevo was an entirely different formation, and there was someone nicknamed Carli who was among them. But when these individuals were in Bijeljina -- well, they weren't deployed in Bijeljina. They were deployed in Brcko. These were Red Berets units headed by Zika, who was also known as Crnogorac or the Montenegrin. They would sometimes go to Bijeljina, cause disturbances, disrupted law and order, and they probably spent some time there when they had time available or when they were looking for something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any connection or relationship between that group of Red Berets and the Arkan's men that were in -- operating in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew each other. They were in contact. But as to the sort of relationship they had, I wouldn't know. I do know that they knew each other and that they did not threaten each other. They did not pose a risk to each other, a danger to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This group of Red Berets that we're talking about now, were they associated or affiliated with any government agency?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I object to that question. Number one, it's leading. Number two, if there's to be any evidence of this nature, it's elicited -- it's better elicited, Your Honour, with the witness informing the Court as to what he might know about the topic, as opposed to a question that is formulated in this leading fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied, Ms. Loukas. The witness may answer the question. The question was whether the group of Red Berets that you're talking about, whether they were associated or affiliated with any government agency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether they were affiliated with a government agency. I know that they had been instructed to go there. The republican MUP in Serbia sent them there. And I know that representatives from Brcko told me that before that they had been -- before they had been sent there, they had had talks with Bogdanovic in Serbia. He was the president of the Council for Security of the Presidency in Serbia and he enabled the Red Berets to go to Brcko. Similarly, when these conflicts broke out, when we arrested them and handed them over to go to Serbia, I know that there were problems and I know that Frenki was unhappy and he phoned on two occasions to ask how it was that I had the right to act in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask, then, two additional questions: Who was Frenki?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frenki was someone from the republican MUP who leaded those units. He was their superior and they reported to him. He was in the police -- secret service and he was one of Mr. Jovica Stanisic's assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any family name of Frenki?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the second question is: How do you know that the republican MUP in Serbia sent them there? And "there" is, as far as I understand, the area of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had been sent to Brcko. That's where they had their headquarters. But sometimes they would go to Bijeljina because it's only 40 kilometres away. But how is it that I knew who they were? Crnogorac -- I took the official identity card from Zika Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Please listen to the question. The question was: How do you know that they were sent by the republican MUP in Serbia? So how do you know that they were sent by them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Crisis Staff in Brcko informed me of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis. Oh, yes, Judge Hanoteau has a question as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have the following question I would like to put to you: In order to understand who these paramilitary forces were under, on page 19 of your statement, paragraph 77 -- 76 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said: [In English] "The paramilitaries had initially been invited -- had been invited in by the local Crisis Staffs. All of the regular police not aligned to the Crisis Staff or the SDS had been removed by the Crisis Staff. So the remaining police were really not functioning." [Interpretation] And further on, you say -- a little further on you say: [In English] The Crisis Staffs lost control of them, so the paramilitaries did whatever they wanted, such as killings, lootings, and so on." [Interpretation] So I would like to understand the exact role that the Crisis Staffs had to play, and I would also like to know whether one can continue to confirm that these paramilitary forces were under the MUP. I believe that there is some confusion as far as this matter is concerned and I would like to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Brcko is concerned, there weren't enough police to maintain public law and order, and that is probably the reason for which they had requested that additional forces be sent in in order to establish power there. And the units that came at the request of the local Crisis Staff, which was in charge of the entire situation, they would supervise the situation in the MUP and they would supervise the paramilitary formations that came from outside. Those units were there to assist the staff and to help at the front lines. That was their role. It wasn't their role to act -- to perform police duties. They were to engage in the armed conflict between the opposing sides. That was their role. But when they arrived there, they would first be under the Crisis Staff -- they would be placed under the Crisis Staff, but then they withdrew. They formed their own staff and they did whatever they believed they were allowed to do. And I think that the Crisis Staff then lost control over them. They could no longer control them. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when these paramilitary forces arrived there, they were initially placed under the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And later, they liberated themselves from this authority and the Crisis Staff lost control over them. They started to act as an independent force. Is that what you are trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. They started acting as an independent force, and someone had probably authorised them to act in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean that the Republic of Serbia MUP was in full control of these formations and instructed them as to how to act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were no longer controlled by the Crisis Staffs but they remained under the control of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite certain. Under the control of the -- of the Republic of Serbia MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, in connection with the Brcko Crisis Staff and the matter we were just discussing, I would direct you to paragraph 106 and following in his statement, where he does give some details about what you were just asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've talked a little bit about the -- the Red Berets that were coming into Bijeljina. Arkan's men, can you tell us, if you know, if Arkan was subordinated to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to these questions about who's subordinate to who and what have you, to ask a question of that nature, which on the experience that we've had thus far with a witness tends to result in an assertion, without a basis in evidence or a foundation for that assertion, I would submit is not of a great deal of assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The evidence is coming out in the form of assertion, without a basis in evidence or a basis for the knowledge of these particular factors that might lead one to an opinion of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the Chamber will not -- not give weight to opinions unless there's a good reason to accept that a witness could have an opinion on something which might be relevant. Ms. Loukas, but at the same time, if you start asking about the source of knowledge without even knowing what you're talking about, of course it's very practical to ask the witness a question like this one and then, of course, as is always done - and I would disagree with you that it's usually done unsuccessful - and then to find out exactly what the source of his knowledge is. You may proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I take on board what Your Honour has indicated. But as long as a mere assertion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- just left there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you may have the experience now that if it's just a mere assertion that, if not the parties, then at least the Chamber always tries to find what the basis of such an assertion is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And will not just leave it somewhere in the air. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, my question was: Do you -- do you know if Arkan was subordinated to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was subordinated to -- well, partly to the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia, to Mico Stanisic, and I assume that President Krajisnik -- or, rather, Mr. Karadzic were aware of his activities and that he also had to report to the Republic of Serbia MUP because he was allowed to come and go, to transport items, to bring in people, transport weapons, equipment. This -- these items were taken across borders in a totally legal way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the basis for your -- your opinion? Anything other than the fact that he was able to transport items across the border?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can we split up this. There are two issues in the answer of the witness. The first one is the -- being subordinate to the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia. I'd like you to find the source of knowledge for that. And then we come to the second part, which is the knowledge, not subordination, by specifically Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'm looking at your answer, and you initially said you thought that he was subordinated partly to the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia, and then you said Mico Stanisic. Let me clear that up first. Mico Stanisic, as I understand it, was in the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior. Jovica Stanisic was in the Serbian MUP, Republic of Serbia. Can you tell me which Stanisic and which republic you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Mico Stanisic in mind, the Ministry -- the Minister of the Interior in the Republika Srpska, because he was familiar with Arkan's activities in the territory of Bijeljina and he knew what he was involved in. Secondly, when I spoke about the extent to which he was responsible to the republican -- the Republic of Serbia MUP, well, I know that he would cross the borders in a legal way. He would introduce himself. He would show his papers. And he would not be obstructed. So he had received authorisation from the republican MUP to act in such a way, because if you want to cross the border, you have to have the necessary papers. To enter the Republic of Serbia, you also need papers for the goods, for the vehicle, and for weapons too. If you don't have authorisation from the MUP, it wouldn't have been possible for him to function in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Judge, I haven't forgotten your request. I'm going to get to the second part in a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mico Stanisic was aware of Arkan's activities. How do you know that he was aware?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told me so himself. He said that Arkan's forces were in Bijeljina and Zvornik. And when I was in the Lukavica barracks, when I was in Sarajevo for the first time with Mico Stanisic, he said that Arkan's forces were helping them to liberate territory that they believed should become part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the second matter I wanted to ask you was: You had indicated earlier in your answer that Radovan Karadzic was -- had knowledge of this. What was your source of information that Mr. Karadzic knew about Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mico Stanisic informed me of that. And on a number of occasions, I was in Sarajevo and Pale and Vrace when contact was established, and the people I was with spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mico Stanisic tell you anything else about Arkan's presence in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special, except that they were engaged there and that they had his approval to help out in the area and that there was agreement amongst themselves that whatever they liberated and took would be an area in which they could do as they liked with any property, any war booty, and that they could use and take anything they felt they could and should. So it would have been their war booty, and that would have been the price to pay for their engagement there, in the area of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have I addressed your questions, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I have one additional question in this respect if you've finished with it. Mr. Davidovic, one of your earlier answers was: "And I assume that President Krajisnik -- or, rather, Mr. Karadzic were aware of his activities." Now, you switched from President Krajisnik to Karadzic, and then you said "were aware." You didn't say "was aware" but "were aware." I want to clearly understand your testimony by saying Mr. -- President Krajisnik -- or, rather, Mr. Karadzic, did you intend to say that you have no knowledge of either Mr. Krajisnik or President Krajisnik being aware? So did you exclude him by turning to Mr. Karadzic? Or do I have to understand your testimony in any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not ruling out either of them. Without their knowledge, without that knowledge on the part of both of them, this would not have been possible. I think both Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic were fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But do you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we now received some nice French translation. We're back on track in English. But do you have any specific reason -- I do understand your testimony. It could not happen without them knowing about it. But do you have any positive -- any information which positively identifies Mr. Krajisnik as being aware of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit I've been asked this before. What can you say about Mr. Krajisnik? I must admit that throughout my work and throughout my experiences, in spite of the fact that this is not a very nice thing to say, I have not managed to spot anything positive about him in the course of his work, in terms of him trying to promote democracy or solve problems. So I must admit I have not a single word of praise I can say about Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not asked about whether you like Mr. Krajisnik's character or not. The question is: Where you say that Mr. Krajisnik and Karadzic were aware, whether you have any specific reason to say that, that any -- that you see anything, that you hear anything from themselves? Did you hear anything from someone else? Or is it just that you say, "Well, it could not have been without their knowledge that this happened"? Then it's purely a conclusion of the events, rather than any specific information you received about their awareness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was directly involved in a number of conversations in Bosnia and in Belgrade where both of them were present, and I was sitting with people -- other people, waiting for talks on the same topic. And Frenki was there and Arkan was there, and I was a witness. I was present in the course of those talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you be -- please be more specific. You said you were sitting with people, waiting for talks on the same topic. You're sitting with what people? You told us Frenki and Arkan. Were you sitting with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was at Bosanska Vila with Mr. Mico Stanisic, Pero Mihajlovic, and Frenki and Arkan was there as well, and so I was present in the course of the talks. And it was in the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where at that moment was Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was on the premises of Bosanska Vila. There was an office there, as soon as you go into the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how do you link Mr. Krajisnik being present in the Bosanska Vila with any talks on involvement or -- of Mr. -- of Arkan or involved with any talks with Arkan himself, if that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whilst we were there at Bosanska Vila, whilst we were sitting down waiting for those talks, there was a kind of preparation for us and the federal SUP and the units that the State Security Service that Frenki was in charge of would be sending down, and Arkan came in with his people and his people were there as well in the course of those talks, and we all talked together and there was a distribution of tasks being decided, who was supposed to do what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Talks to be held exactly between who and who? Were these talks where Mr. Krajisnik and Arkan were both present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I'm saying. President Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said tasks were distributed. Could you give us an example of such a task to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, as a federal SUP, we went to Pale to the Republika Srpska in the first place to provide assistance with special units and provide equipment; whereas, Frenki was in charge of units that had other tasks, in terms to help MUP against the enemy and Arkan did what he felt was understood between him and Krajisnik and Karadzic and Mico Stanisic and the local staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that -- the task of Arkan was to do what he felt was understood between him and Krajisnik and Karadzic and Stanisic. How do you -- what was this, said to him, or -- could you just describe how that specific task was discussed at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stress once again: I was present on the occasion when we got there to hold talks about the needs and the role of the federal SUP and all the other units present there. They all, within their own area of competence, held talks with Mico Stanisic, Krajisnik, and Karadzic, and everybody did what they felt should be their contribution in the part of the work that they were supposed to carry out. So we were assigned the task that I've just told you about, and Mr. Arkan did what he was authorised to do, probably by Karadzic and Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what words was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said, "Okay. Let's help here. What can you do? Or don't interfere with that. This is somebody else's area of competence." So this was the kind of language that was used. Or, "Drop that. We are in charge of that. Don't interfere. What can you do," et cetera, in terms of individual topics being determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So he was not provided positively with tasks, but it was told to him, if I correctly understand you, to stay out of certain matters, which you understood to be that he was free to do what was not prohibited specifically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I can follow up on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This meeting that you've been talking about, do you know approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992. It could have been April or May, at Bosanska Vila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if it was before or after Arkan's men had entered Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to go back to your statement, Mr. Davidovic, and talk about paragraph 82. This is in July, when you've gone to Bijeljina to deal with the paramilitary problem. You say: "I received documents signed by Cedo Kljajic from the RS MUP authorising me to operate as the chief of police affairs in the RS." My first question is: What was that position, chief of police affairs in Republika Srpska? That's not a title I've heard before in connection with police work. Was that a regular job, or was that a special title created just for you on this occasion, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is a job for the chief of police within the MUP of the republic. That's an office for the chief of the police officers, uniformed police, and he's accountable to the person in charge of national security. And it's a fairly high-ranking job because it is a person -- the person in charge of all the police forces within the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in that regard, then, in the -- in the chain of command or the hierarchical structure, who would you, as chief of police affairs, be required to report to in Republika Srpska? Who was the boss for the chief of police affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cedo Kljajic would be the first boss, and then Mico Stanisic, as the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to you as chief of police affairs, did you have authority over other members -- all other members of the MUP? Who were you the boss of, then, as chief of police affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given that title, as it were, simply in order to provide me with the authority to act whenever I visited a body from the MUP of the republic, say Lopare, Zvornik, Brcko. If anyone were to ask me who gave me the authority to go there, I think for that reason I was given that title in order to give me the authority to act and to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you could give -- issue -- you could issue orders to heads of local police stations or heads of police centres, such as in Bijeljina or Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the area that I was working in, Central Bosnia, or any other area, but only in the area where I was at any given time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 84, you talk about your meeting with Colonel Ilic from the VRS to talk about working together on dealing with the problem on paramilitaries. And in your statement in paragraph 84, you say he told you that "The paramilitaries were not under the control of the army and that they had the full support of the SDS." Did he tell you how he knew that or what he based that opinion on, that these paramilitaries had the support of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Ilic was a corps commander and their area of responsibility was Central Bosnia, and he was in charge of all armed units which were both the police and the army. They were both under his control. And he was able to issue orders to police as well, and we had to follow his orders. So it was quite clear what units were under his command and who he could issue orders to and who not, and he said to me in so many words, with regard to the situation in the city of Bijeljina, where Mauzer was in command. And then at Brcko, somebody called Tito was in charge there. And then at Zvornik, Zuco and Repic were there. And at Ugljevik, there was a Mando, who was heading some technical formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you what his source of knowledge was for the assertion that these paramilitaries apparently had the full support of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a commander, he had to know who was subjected -- subordinated to him and who he should issue orders to. It is the first thing you must know as commander. And the fact that he was unable to influence the decisions or issue orders to units with regard to the guard, well, it is enough to indicate that he did not have authority to issue instructions or orders to those units, as to what they're supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you're talking about the guard, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard unit that was set up at Bijeljina. It was a kind of party army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the direction of whom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, it was considered that SDS had to set up their own units and that they should be the ones in charge of any future war or other operations. And Bijeljina was the first place where it was done. The whole process was initiated at Bijeljina. Their main task and main aim was, as they said, to defend the Serb people, and only members of the SDS party could become members of that unit. And yeah, only they could join the guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Who was the leader of the guard in Bijeljina? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Savic, called Mauzer. And afterwards there were some other changes. But it was at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 85, you talk about --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just prior to moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just at the beginning of page 19 of the transcript, the -- the answer is given: "Well, as commander, he had to know who was subjected -- subordinated to him ...." I'm given to understand that there's a nuance of translation there that may not have come across, in the sense that it would be ought to have known or should have known, as opposed to he had to know. And perhaps that might be clarified, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters have -- could you -- when you said, as it is translated to us: "As a commander" -- and you were talking about Mr. Ilic -- "he had to know who was subjected, subordinated to him," whether you would say this is what he should know or what inevitably he must have known, if that correctly, Ms. Loukas -- it's a very subtle linguistic matter. So as a non-native speaker, I hope that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I'll just indicate what our understanding is that the word used was. And the word was "valjda."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're very close to the microphone, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, "valjda."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Supposedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Supposedly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I might get my legal assistant to actually say it so that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the interpreters, if you had -- they have said that they would translate it as "supposedly."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the matter having been clarified. I would have, apart from this objection, I would have one question: You said "only members of the SDS could join the guard. How do you know exactly -- did you know exactly who were members of the SDS and, at the same time, joined this guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew who members of the SDS were and who was joining the guard. In the last analyses, they were registered. The guard was set up on the basis of the members who were close to the leadership of the Crisis Staff at Bijeljina, and people who registered with that unit mostly went through training that was organised by Arkan at Bogatic, on the border between Bijeljina and the Republic of Serbia, along the River Drina, where there were training centres. And that was the core of that future guard unit. And then they took volunteers from the entire municipality who came along and joined the unit. But -- but only and exclusively members of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have access to the registers in which they were listed, or would that also include those who were in favour of or supporting the SDS even if there would be no members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the opportunity to have access to the documents when we were at Bijeljina. We took their centre where their command post was, and I found documents there that later on I submitted to Mr. Ilic, who was the corps commander, and those documents included the list of people who joined the guard unit. And that's how I knew. Secondly, for 20 years I had been within the police force at Bijeljina, and I knew very many people, and especially people who became active in the Serb Democratic Party and engaged in other activities afterwards, and that's how I knew. And when the guard was first set up, it was only made up of members of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your conclusion that the guard members were exclusively SDS members, you concluded that from their previous activities in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau has ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a municipality such as Bijeljina, sir, what would have been the ratio or the number of people joining the SDS? Since you said that you knew many people in the community, how many women and men would have joined the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, it is very hard to tell at the moment in terms of percentages. I think it's -- well, nigh impossible. I don't really want to play with figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I want to move to paragraph 85 in your statement, where you talk about Colonel Ilic showing you a telegram that his chief of security, one Tanaskovic, had sent apparently inquiring about what authority you had to arrest military personnel as well as civilians. And I -- and you say that Tolimir had replied to that telegram. Did Tolimir tell you -- or do you know what Tolimir had said in response to that telegram inquiring about your authority?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got to the corps to see Ilic for the first time, he said to me that Tolimir had called him and he asked about whether he knew about this message he got from Tanaskovic. I think he was a major or a lieutenant colonel who was in charge of security within the corps. Because of his line of work, he sent a telegram, a message to Mr. Tolimir, who was the head of security for the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska, and he asked him who I was and whether I had any authority and how -- who gave me the authority to arrest military personnel when they were caught stealing or looting, et cetera. And he told him and he confirmed that I did have such an authority when it was about crime, whether it is being committed by civilians or military staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a couple of documents now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the next item could be given a number. This is a 4th of July document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But is this in relation to your last question or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number will be P771.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'll ask you to have a look at this. I'm not sure how legible the B/C/S copy is. Once you've had a chance to look at that, would you tell us if you've seen it before or if you know what it relates to.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before, but I know that this was sent to Tolimir, and yes, that is the dispatch in question. In fact, the first time I saw it was when you showed it to me a couple of days ago. But I know that this is a dispatch sent to Colonel Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I note that in the heading, it is addressed to the Serb BiH Presidency and also to the Serb BiH Ministry of Internal Affairs. Did -- did anyone contact you about this telegram, other than your conversation with Colonel Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mico Stanisic asked me what it was about, and I told him. He said, to the extent that this was possible, one should avoid officers, members of the military, being taken into the MUP. He believed that the military police should do such things. He said I shouldn't really take action when it came to members of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you the next document, which is from the 5th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can give that a number and hand it to you. It also pertains to this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be P772.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were first assigned this task to come to Bijeljina and deal with the paramilitaries, what were you told was going to be your authority? And I mean back in -- in Belgrade, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry? You didn't hear my question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I really do apologise. I wasn't concentrating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Before you came to Bijeljina to deal with the paramilitaries, when you were given that assignment back in -- in Serbia, when you were in the federal MUP, what were you told would be your power or your authority, in terms of dealing with the problem? Were you going to be limited in any way as to who you could arrest and not arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had the authority to disarm paramilitary formations, and they did not specify whether these were civilian or -- civilians or members of the military. That was my task before I arrived there. And a couple of days earlier, I went to the MUP in Bijeljina and saw Cedo Kljajic there and we agreed on the responsibilities that I would have. We agreed on all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a look at Exhibit 772, which has just been handed to you now. And does this relate to the -- the matter that we were just talking about, regarding a complaint about you arresting military members?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm familiar with this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did -- did you take any action as a result of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, we had a joint plan with the military police in Bijeljina. We agreed on the measures to be taken. And I remember that the commander of the military police at the time, Stevanovic - I don't know what his first name was, but his nickname was Ceco - he was in charge. He had contact with me with regard to the future action to be taken by both the civilian and military police. Cveto Stevanovic, also known as Ceco. He was the chief of the corps police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to move a little farther in your statement. We're still talking about the acts in Bijeljina. In paragraph 95, you say that Mauzer had set up a private gaol at the slaughter-house, and you're talking about going to those premises with the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we mark the next item and give it the next number. It's the 7 of July document, described as a "Report on inspection."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P773.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what that is. Have you seen it before? What does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was compiled by officials from Bijeljina who were present at the on-site investigation. When we were in Bijeljina, we entered the premises of a refrigeration facility because we knew that certain individuals were being detained there. This was a private prison, and Mauzer was in charge. When we got there, we saw certain individuals in the slaughter-house, in the refrigeration facilities. We took them out of the building and made it possible for them to go home unhindered. Quite a lot of goods that had been stolen in Brcko were taken. And this document refers to what was found there and to the individuals found there. So you can quite clearly see what we did. And the prosecutor was also informed of this. He was present too. After we had taken those over facilities, both the civilian prosecutor and the military prosecutor went to the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that this was reported to the public prosecutor, the federal SUP, and to the RS MUP in your statement. Were any arrests or prosecutions instituted as a result of this on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We drafted a criminal report and forwarded a report to the MUP. I informed the federal MUP as well. But as far as I know, no action was taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- the five Muslims that are described in that on-site investigation, I think you've just told us, were -- were released and allowed to go home. Do you have any information about why they were detained there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that your involvement in this activity did not ingratiate you with Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our relationship deteriorated. I became that unit's main enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you the next item on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I would like to clarify something with regard to the Serb voluntary guard. Could you tell us approximately how many men this paramilitary group was composed of? Could you provide us with a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the first day, when this group was established -- there were 224 of them in the line when the brigade was formed in Bijeljina. There were 224 of them. That includes the officers. And later there were over 1.000 men. I don't know how many exactly, but they said that they -- they had over 1.000 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were these men recruited initially? The 220 men, where were they recruited? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this unit was formed, the men were all from Bijeljina. I mean, the municipality of Bijeljina, not the town of Bijeljina. And at the time, the municipality had a lot of inhabitants. They were all from Bijeljina, and there were no men who came from outside Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we had a late start. We need two breaks anyhow, because one break would not do. If you could find within the next couple of minutes a suitable moment for a break, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is as good as any time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 25 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Hannis proceeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I just want to foreshadow -- and, of course, the witness is present in court, so I won't deal with the matter. But I do want to foreshadow that prior to the next break, I just want to deal briefly with the question of material relating to a forthcoming witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll find some time before the next break. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, when we broke, you had just mentioned that your relations with Mauzer and his group had deteriorated. I want to show you the next two documents, from 7 and 8 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If they could be given consecutive numbers and both of them handed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They'll be P774 and P775.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P775, I take it, for the 7th of July; and P775 for the 8th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While those are being handed round, Your Honour, may I ask a scheduling question. Since we started late because of the technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I ask what time we're going to today. The usual quitting time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a -- as far as scheduling for interpreters and technicians are concerned. Unless, Madam Registrar, we would have more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar will check whether -- how tight we are limited to quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the time for the next break, Your Honour, given our late start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, of course, I would like to first hear the information from Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But usually I split it up in two parts, the second part being a bit shorter than the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, could you look first at that document dated, I think, the 7th of July, entitled "An official note," and compiled by a person named Dragan Andan. First of all, could you remind us -- it's in your statement, but could you remind us briefly who was Dragan Andan? Who did he work for? What was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Andan worked in the republican MUP before the war as a police inspector. And when I arrived in the Central Bosnia area, in Bijeljina, I was then informed by Kljajic that Dragan Andan was to act as a coordinator between me and the republican MUP. He was to act as a coordinator between Cedo Kljajic and myself as a representative of the federal MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at this feast --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever we talk about the republican MUP, could we please always specify whether we are talking about BiH -- Republika Srpska republican MUP or Serbia republican MUP, in order to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will -- I will do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And regarding your last answer, that republican MUP, which republic were you referring to, and Mr. Kljajic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And his note -- well, first of all, let me ask you: Were you present at this feast day that's described in this note?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you the document 775, the other one that was handed to you from the 8th of July. Have you had a chance to look at that one yet? This is one that was compiled by Sinisa --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had a look at it yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do. Tell us who Sinisa Karan was.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Karan was also an employee in the former MUP in the BH, and later he moved to Republika Srpska and he was appointed as a commander of the police station in Bijeljina. Cedo Kljajic appointed him to that post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he describes events that occurred to him as part of a team that included you, Dragan Andan, and a BH government representative named as Jovo Miskel [phoen]. Do you recall that event? Is it accurately described here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mention the name here appears as Miskel. I note in your statement at paragraph 97 you refer to someone who appears to be the same individual as Miskin. Do you know which name is correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jovo Miskin. That was the person's name. He was in charge of Bijeljina. He was responsible for Bijeljina, and he was a government commissioner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why the -- the Serbian National Guard was trying to stop your -- your team?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. They wanted to have the freedom to do what they were involved in, looting, looting items from Muslims in the territory of Bijeljina, in territory under their control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly was -- was Mauzer's status with the Crisis Staff in Bijeljina at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mauzer was the president of the Crisis Staff at the beginning of the war, the president of the Crisis Staff was -- Stjepan was the president of the Assembly and he was the president of the Crisis Staff, and perhaps a month later Mauzer was appointed as president of the Crisis Staff and he was the president of the Crisis Staff in Bijeljina, and he was in charge of a guard unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I gather from your statement that you -- you had information indicating that his unit had been involved in criminal activity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And given your mandate and authority from the -- from the federal SUP when you game to Bijeljina and from the RS MUP, as chief of police affairs, how was Mauzer able to continue to be such a problem for you? Why couldn't you simply arrest him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, Mauzer stopped doing what he was involved in, but he tried to expel us. He requested that we be expelled from territory and the Crisis Staff requested that I leave. He asked this to happen. During that period of time, he refrained from taking any action because he knew that strident measures would be taken against him. If I had expected him to do anything, I would have arrested him immediately and filed a criminal report against him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- you talk about that in paragraph 99 of your statement, that the Municipal Assembly passed a resolution in which they demanded that you be expelled from the municipality. Who -- who told you about that? How did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the decision -- I was informed of the decision by the president of the Executive Committee of the Assembly and by Dr. Vojinovic. They said that a decision had been taken according to which I should be expelled from the territory and I should be banned from taking any further action in that area. And on Radio Bijeljina it was quite publicly stated that I should be prevented from staying in Bijeljina since I was protecting Muslims. They said I was an old Communist and that that was from a bygone period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did -- did this resolution or this effort to try and get you expelled from Bijeljina stop with just that municipal resolution?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. As far as I know, representatives from the -- a representative from the republican parliament, Micic, told me that they had discussed the matter at the republican parliament and they wanted an example to be set with regard to confronting these paramilitary formations. However, they nevertheless decided that I should be prevented from taking further action and a request was made for me to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you next --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, I'd like to have these two next exhibits marked with the consecutive numbers. The first is the 29 July report by RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P776.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then there is a letter from Andan with an attached report dated also the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I've skipped one on your list. Number 19 is not the one I want to do right now. I want to do 21 and 22, if I may. Sorry, Ms. Javier. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything is clear, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So the numbers still remain the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The same numbers are assigned to those two documents respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, this is a document that you have seen before and actually the report -- they are two different copies. The reason you're being shown two is because there's some handwritten information on one that I want to ask you about. Would you have a look at the last page of that document. And if you -- can you recognise that the name and signature that appears there is the sender of the report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me, I don't know who wrote this and whose signature this is, and I can't even tell what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I see -- I'm not asking you about the three handwritten lines at the bottom; however, the signature that appears under the typewritten name above that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch what the witness has just said. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat for the interpreter, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the signature of Dragan Andan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oh, actually no -- yes, I had seen it before, but not with this signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the front page, it's described as "Information about the involvement and activities of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before you proceed, it's not the first time that you ask whether the witness has seen a document before. Could you please always verify whether he has never seen it before, whether he has seen it last week, or at any earlier stage. Because in view of the practice by the OTP, it would be highly surprising if a witness would not have seen such a document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you first saw this document or a document that contained this kind of information about the security situation in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was created by Dragan Andan in my presence basically. Novica Terzic [phoen] obtained the information here. He also worked for the federal SUP and he was an analyst. And he was sent to us -- to me, actually, as an assistant because of operational duties I had to carry out, I just did not have time to put it all in writing and make it into an official document, and for this reason he was asked to come and assist me in that task and compile this document, including the information as to what we had been doing. And this was done following a request from the Municipal Assembly, and it was discussed at the Municipal Assembly when there was a discussion about the general role and activities of SUP at that time. And this is the information that was rejected by the Municipal Assembly. They did not want to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the information in here describes the various kinds of criminal activity that had been occurring prior to the engagement of -- of your men and personnel from the Republika Srpska MUP. If I understand what you're saying, this report was compiled based on information provided by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did that and Dragan as well, who worked with me. We gathered that information when we got there, and so basically it includes the results of our operational work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Terzic was the analyst with the specialised writing ability who actually composed the document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novica Terzic was an employee at the federal secretariat of the Ministry of the Interior and he worked within the police force, the secret services, and he was in charge of analyses, and he was -- I don't want to say that he was specially gifted, but he knew how to process all that information very swiftly, and he could do this fast. And he was an expert. I didn't want to say that he was gifted. He was actually an expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at -- there is one copy of the document that has a handwritten name, "Cedo," on the front. Can you -- can you locate that one? I think one of those two exhibits you've been handed - I believe it's 776 - has a handwritten name on the first page at the top. It's translated as "Cedo."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Ministry of Internal Affairs at that time, who would have been the Cedo that that copy would be going to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Cedo Kljajic, who was the assistant secretary. And we did send the information to him. We had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the other document, 777, which has a cover letter from Mr. Andan that's addressed to the president of the Presidency, Mr. Karadzic. And I will tell you that the handwritten material after Mr. Andan's signature at the end of the report has been translated as reading: "Keep enforcing order and rule of law. 2 August 1992. Radovan Karadzic." You said you didn't recognise that signature or the writing. Do you have any reason to disbelieve that that's Mr. Karadzic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not an appropriate way of asking the question. It's simply the -- what appears there appears there. The witness has indicated that -- he's given his answer in relation to the handwriting. For Mr. Hannis to attempt to introduce evidence in relation to this document in this manner is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, the absence of any disbelief, would that support in any way that it is Mr. Krajisnik's -- Mr. Karadzic's signature? Apart from that one out of how many million people of the world would not have a reason to believe that it's not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess I just wanted to enquire whether he had any reason that I'm not aware of to think that it's a forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To that extent, Ms. Loukas, of course Mr. Hannis is aware that it will be his duty to -- to establish that it was Mr. Karadzic's handwriting in one way or the other. And at the same time, if there would be any reason to doubt, he'd like to know so that he could take that into consideration. And I take it that's important for the Defence as well, if there's any reason to believe it would not be Mr. Karadzic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then that's, I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The point is that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- sufficiently --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- question is inappropriately asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are not a jury. I have, however, Mr. -- if, once you've finished with the documents, I'd like to ask something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I had a couple of other questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- but I can await for your question because you may address something I was going to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you wanted to address it not. But I take it that we have 776 as a copy of a report just, and then 777 as a copy of the report with a letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then some handwriting at the bottom, which might demonstrate that someone has seen it at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it has the cover sheet, which I'm not sure is on the other one that has "Cedo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I have a totally different problem. Where these documents are supposed to be the same, I'm a bit surprised to see that in 777 the letter bears the letterhead of "Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and the report has the heading of "Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," which in translation surprises me a bit. I am able now to decipher some obvious even Cyrillic B/C/S. If I compare that with the other document, it says "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," which is of course something different than -- it looks very much as -- it starts with "Srpska Republika" on both the cover letter and the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. And I noticed there were some other differences in the body of the text between those two English versions. The 777 is a CLSS translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: However, that's the one that's described as Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have some difficulty -- of course, I'm not a linguistic expert, but reading "Srpska Republika Bosnia-Herzegovina," very much sounds not as Federal Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. And had you not raised that point, Your Honour, I would have been asking you to -- let's use the CLSS translation as the one. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you'd -- if you'd finally make up your mind and -- and then attach at least the valid translation to each of the documents so that there could be no confusion, even if you think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The purpose of 776 was to show that a copy had gone to a member of the Republika Srpska MUP, Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honour, it's also been confirmed by my legal assistant, who also speaks B/C/S, that quite clearly the P777 is an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even without this confirmation, Ms. Loukas, the Chamber might have accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Assuming Mr. Hannis takes care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming for purpose of my next question that that is Mr. Karadzic's signature saying "keep on enforcing the rule of law," it would seem to indicate that there was approval from him for the work that you and Mr. Andan had done in Bijeljina. Did you receive any kind of promotion or pay raise or letter of appreciation for the work that you had done in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get a raise or no support in any way. I must admit I did not know about this, and I don't know whether this came from Radovan Karadzic. I mean, this is the document that I had not seen before, and I don't know. But we continued to work. We did not follow the decision of the Assembly and we did not withdraw at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about that. How about Dragan Andan? Did he get any kind of promotion or pay raise or recognition for the work he did --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, certainly not. And certainly not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to put a marker there. It's -- I object to questions of this nature about what on earth the Trial Chamber could make of whether there was a promotion or a pay-rise and how relevant that is to the Trial Chamber's consideration is hard to fathom from the Defence perspective, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes - I'm not saying always, Ms. Loukas - pay-rise reflects a higher level of appreciation of the work done. So we could not say it could under no circumstances be relevant. But if there's no pay-rise, then, of course, it doesn't say that much. The relevance is in the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now you say it becomes irrelevant through the answer. That's not the proper way of approaching it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Mr. Hannis has proofed the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's one of the things you always insist, and with good reasons, that the witness should give the evidence. The Chamber is not in a position, and I think you are not in a position either, to know whether the answer surprised Mr. Hannis or not. And it's the relevance of the question that counts. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to come back to a previous part of the statement. I would like to go back to para 100, on page 24. You have indicated, sir, that the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly [In English] "had demanded my removal." And according to Micic, with the deputy of the Assembly, not of the Municipal Assembly, [Interpretation] but of the Assembly of the Republic, according to this Micic, it would appear that there had been a debate, a discussion at the Assembly at the end of which it transpired that you were supposed to be placed under tight control and that your activities should be restricted. Was that the case? Your case was looked into at two different levels, at the Municipal Assembly and at the Assembly of the Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, it was discussed at the Municipal Assembly and there were differences of opinion amongst delegates or representatives, as they were called then, and some were in favour of me continuing with my work and others were against it. But there was this person called Micic, who was also in favour of my continuing. I don't know. Perhaps he believed that having proper law and order would have a positive effect on policies afterwards. I don't know what led him to believe that, but he did think that what I did was a good thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was your feeling at the time? It appears as if at the time you were put in a somewhat weird position. You were officially seconded there and allocated to carry out certain tasks, and it appears as if a part of that -- of those official duties were being argued against by people who were in positions of power. Could you tell us how you interpreted it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit that I felt very uncomfortable. I mean, of course if a local community asks you to withdraw and your main aim is to introduce law and order, I mean, instead of people asking me to continue, they're arguing against my work. But if you keep in mind that Mauzer, who was the president of the Crisis Staff, and he had a group of people around him who were the leaders within the Assembly and that the SDS was the leading and the only party making any decisions within that Municipal Assembly, I had no reason to expect that I would gain any support whatsoever. But another essential point is that it was not the Municipal Assembly that put me there. I did not come there following their request. I went there within the framework of my job somewhere else. And I was not even accountable to them in any way. I was not either subordinated or anything. I did not have a formal relationship with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in that case, when Mr. Micic told you about that discussion at the Assembly, did he tell you that within the Assembly there were differing opinions, considering your activities and your way of doing things in general? Had there been a discussion in the course of which totally different opinions were being voiced? I mean, what did Mr. Micic tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you briefly. He did say that there were differing opinions, but most people were negative, and especially the representative from Lopare, Mr. Perovic, was of the view that I had no reason to be there because I was a leftover from previous times, from Communist times, and that I should be removed no matter what I did and how I did it. And I can give you another interesting detail in this respect. It's slightly uncomfortable. I wouldn't like to highlight it in any way. Micic said - and he even apparently said it out loud on the occasion of that Municipal Assembly - that we would live to regret what we are doing now, at the time when we neglected to give him full support and full authority. And he meant myself. And he said, "We are going to make a statue of him out of clay and -- just so to be able to hope that his positive work will have some kind of impact and some kind of lasting effect." Well, that's what he said to me. I don't know whether he actually did say that during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional matter to raise, Mr. Hannis. This part of the statement is redacted. Nevertheless, the Chamber expects under those circumstances, if the statement gives any information, that it will be elicited orally from the witness, and is specifically interested in this part because it is hearsay but if in the transcript of any of the Assembly sessions this would appear, then of course what the witness said might gain, because it gets a far better basis. If, on the other hand, it would not appear, then of course Ms. Loukas would, I would say, with reason say, "Here you see how dangerous hearsay evidence is." So the Chamber is very much interested to see whether verification on the basis of documents would either strengthen or considerably weaken the -- the information of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my information -- I understand your point. My information in that regard is that for this Assembly session, which we believe was either August or September of 1992, is one for which we do not have a full transcript. We only have the minutes of the session. And I can tell you that I -- there's not a reference to Mr. Davidovic's name in -- in the minutes of the session, but this is not one -- this is one of those sessions where we don't have the full line-by-line transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you'd say that it remains uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the minutes say anything about it, even without mentioning a name sometimes. But I just wanted to point at the opportunity we might have either to find further confirmation or the contrary of this witness's statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
