utterances.text: One more thing on that, Your Honour. I did look at the minutes to see if there was something on the agenda, in terms of a topic that might have covered this. There is one that's kind of a common one, oftentimes a report on the general security situation in -- in the republic. Other than that, I don't believe there was anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on, then, if there are no more questions regarding that. In addition to you being the subject of a motion or a resolution in the Municipal Assembly to be expelled, you say in your statement at paragraph 97 that "The Municipal Assembly also called for Mr. Miskin's removal and expulsion from Bijeljina." What had he done that caused them to ask for him to be expelled? He was not a policeman. He was not engaged in arresting Serbs or protecting Muslims, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Miskin was a government commissioner who got -- who was authorised by the government to follow the events in the area of Semberija and to relay the government's position and to report back to the government. Mr. Miskin gave us his full support, but his support actually led to greater resistance within the local community precisely because of the fact that they felt that his support to me meant that he was a person who shouldn't be there either. If he gave his support to me, what was he doing in that local community? They did not trust him because they believed that it was them who knew best and that somebody who had different views and opinions had no place there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I want to move on to another municipality. After Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked about scheduling. We'll continue until 12.50, then have a break until ten minutes past 1.00, and then we could continue until quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you're reviewing the translations anyhow, 776 and 777, where 776 seems to be better -- better as far as the heading is concerned, on one of the pages footnotes are a bit too much. They do not -- they appear more footnotes in the text than appear on the bottom of the page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where -- in your statement it appears that you next went to Brcko. Why did you decide to go to Brcko next instead of Zvornik, which you say was between those two? What decided you for Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local community and the Crisis Staff in Brcko had requested that I come to assist them, disarm paramilitary formations, Red Berets led by Zika Crnogorac. And then there was another paramilitary formation, a local one, under someone called Tito - that was his nickname - because they had lost all control over them and they were acting in a willful way, and this had adverse consequences and the citizens were very unhappy about the situation. It wasn't clear who they were working for and what sort of things they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraphs 102 through 114, you describe how that process went in Brcko and -- and the rather tense confrontation you had with that group before you were able to arrest them. Shortly after you had detained those Red Berets, you got a call from somebody in Belgrade about them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a clash that we had with the Red Berets in Bijeljina. There was a situation there. They arrived in the early morning hours in Bijeljina, and there was a clash between the Red Berets and the Radicals, under Mirko Blagojevic. They entered Mirko Blagojevic's house, where they had a headquarters of some kind. They tied him up. They used handcuffs to tie him up, and they took him to Brcko. When we heard about this armed group that had encircled the house, we went there, intercepted them, and then we clashed with them. Shooting even broke out. We managed to get Mirko Blagojevic out of the house after we had stopped them and we took Mirko Blagojevic to the SUP. And then later they asked what had been done -- they asked me why I had acted like this, since I was part of the MUP. And then I spoke with someone from Belgrade. I think I spoke to Frenki, but I'm not sure of this. And this is what I told you when we first discussed the matter. He asked me, "Who authorised you to do that? What are you doing there? Who sent you there," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you respond to him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I say? I said, "You've sent criminals there to loot and steal things from people and now you want me to pass over that in silence. So what is the purpose of me being here then?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find out about Zika and this group of Red Berets in terms of whether they were sent there by anyone or working for anyone or they were an independent group? What information did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago I spoke about this. The Crisis Staff informed me about the fact that they had requested help. They went to Belgrade. Bogdanovic promised that they would be assisted. And after that discussion, a group was sent to help them, led by Zika Crnogorac. This was information obtained from the Republic of Serbia MUP, because they even had vehicles from the Republic of Serbia MUP. They wore red berets and that is when the Red Berets first became engaged in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And they didn't try to conceal the fact that these forces were their forces under their control. And when we had a clash with them in Brcko, when we tried to drive them out, I asked them to go to Belgrade and to inform Bogdanovic about everything they had done in Brcko and inform him of the reason for which they had requested that they be expelled. I also wanted him to be informed of the fact that they shouldn't be sent back to the area and they should be prevented from acting in the way that they had acted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Red Berets under Zika and another group under Tito. Was Mauzer and his guard involved in any of the activity in Brcko at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. His headquarters was in the hospital in Brcko, and he and his entire unit held the front line from the factory towards Mauca [phoen], I think -- Rahici, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you had finished -- or were able to restore some sort of semblance of law and order, as you mention in paragraph 124 of your statement, in Brcko, where did you go next? What was your next area of operation in trying to deal with the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Zvornik. I became involved in disarming paramilitary formations there under Zuco and his brother Repic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you work with in making plans for this operation to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I also had contact with members of the service in Zvornik, someone who worked in the Security Service would appear. I can't remember his exact name. Similarly, I was visited by people from the Serbian MUP. Mr. Jekic came to see me. He worked in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and he came to see me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also work with Dragan Andan in the Zvornik operation as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was with me all the time and he was also in charge of the operative part of the action they had been assigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document now dated the 20th of July. It's number 19 on the list we've given the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that can be given the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement in paragraph 126 that while you were in Bijeljina, that Mico Stanisic came to see you. About Zvornik, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he told me that there were paramilitary formations in Zvornik under the command of Zuco and certain criminal acts were being admitted there. People who came from Pale were being intercepted. They were stealing vehicles. They were looting. And no one could confront them. He said that at the time they didn't have the possibility to prevent that. They didn't have the forces to prevent such acts. He gave a number of examples of vehicles being seized from individuals passing through the area. And he mentioned some individuals, including Mr. Ostojic, who I think was at the time a Minister of Information in the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reference to Mr. Ostojic about? How did that have a connection with the paramilitaries in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What do you mean "connection"? One of the persons whose vehicle was seized was Mr. Ostojic, and he was then forced to get out of the car. His vehicle was taken. He must have informed the government and requested protection. So that was the climax. That's when the situation came to a head in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make a specific request of you regarding Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he asked for the paramilitary formation to be disarmed. He said that we in the army and the special units from Sarajevo should be engaged. This special unit from Sarajevo should come to the territory and -- and join us in order to disarm the paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document you have in front of you now, have you had a chance to look at that? It's an information on the security situation in Zvornik. And this is also signed by Dragan Andan as head of the Bijeljina CSB. Have you seen that document before -- did you see it around the time that you were preparing to go to Zvornik to deal with the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This information was compiled at that time, when we were supposed to go to Zvornik, and I was one of the persons who was involved in drafting it. Novica Terzic was also involved in the information and Dragan signed it because he was the chief of the station and he had the authority to sign such a document. But I did not subsequently see the document. This is the first time I've seen it since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement at paragraph 129 and 130 that in your initial planning, you were coordinating with the military and you had a team of about 100 men, including the 14 from the federal SUP. Did -- did that team grow to include another agency?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we started preparing the operative action in detail, I was visited in Bijeljina by Colonel or Lieutenant Colonel Salapura, who was from the Main Staff. He was the deputy or assistant of Tolimir. He worked in the Security Service and he provided me with all the information that I already had, information they had obtained, and he asked for these things to be prevented. He suggested that an army unit, a military police unit from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army become engaged, and this unit consisting -- composed of about 50 men was attached to me. So in addition to the unit under my command, there was Salapura, who was present with a military police unit, and I think there was an officer called Pecanac [phoen], who was in charge of that group of 50 men. And there was a special unit from Republika Srpska under the command of Karisik, and there were 150 men in that unit. I was in charge of the entire action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That special unit from the RS MUP under Karisik, was that at your request that they were a part of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. It wasn't at my request. I was even against engaging that unit. I did not trust the men in that unit, although I had known the unit since the time it had been established. I participated in its establishment. But I didn't want it to become involved because I thought that its involvement would have other consequences. And this subsequently proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those other consequences that you were concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was worried about the fact that when the unit arrived in the territory of Zvornik, where there was a lengthy border and where people would cross the state border - that's the main point of entry into Republika Srpska - I was concerned about the fact that such a unit would be deployed there. I was concerned about the fact that they might do certain things that resembled things that Zuco and his paramilitary formation did. If they were in Zvornik and after the action had been completed, that unit remained in the Hotel Drina, and in the Hotel Vidikovac at the entrance to Zvornik, and they remained there for two years for sure and they covered the entrance point to Republika Srpska. They monitored all the goods that were going into Republika Srpska and coming out of Republika Srpska, and they were the main people involved in the trade that was spreading at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had reservations about having this unit as a part of the operation. Who -- how did they get to be part of the operation, if you had reservations and didn't want them? How did they come to be imposed on you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was an order issued by Mico Stanisic, the minister. They were to be engaged on the basis of his order, regardless of what my opinion was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had the RS special unit been offered to you to help in Bijeljina or in Brcko, when you were dealing with the paramilitaries in those two locations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason why now, when you were going to Zvornik, they were being made a part of the operation? Was there something different about Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have just explained that. Because it's at the border; it's an important point because goods are exported from Republika Srpska at that point and taken into Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, have you dealt with the documents until now? Are you moving to another subject or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am moving to another one now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would have two short questions. The first, in relation to the document we dealt with last, that is, P778. Do you, Mr. Davidovic, have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you ... Yes, you have got it in front of you. And Madam Usher, would you please prepare 776 for the witness for the next question. Could you please read B/C/S, second page, semi-last paragraph, the last sentence, in which the numbers 350.000 and 500.000 marks appear. Could you please read that last sentence slowly. Could the witness please do that. Could you please read that aloud, second page, B/C/S, semi-last paragraph, last three lines of that paragraph, in which the numbers 350.000 and 500.000 appear. Could you please read that aloud slowly. Mr. Davidovic, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it. What should I read out? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Prior to that occurring, I'm just wondering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- if the Prosecution have a spare copy of the document in question, as Mr. Krajisnik doesn't have the -- the B/C/S version of that particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have one, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can give him mine, of the B/C/S. It doesn't help me much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, could you please read those three lines aloud so that the interpreters can translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Foreign currency, 350.000 German marks were offered for this favour. They were offered by the Green Berets. Whereas, Zuco had requested 500.000 German marks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies the issue. If you would look at the translation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The witness said 500 German marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes well, that's one of the things I can read myself, that it is 500.000. But, Mr. Hannis, the Green Berets offered the sum of 350.000, as far as I now understand, and not asked. So translation should be corrected in this respect. And then suddenly this sentence makes sense, where it did not prior to this correction. Now, the second question I'd like to put to you, Mr. Davidovic: The report on Bijeljina, the first line reads: "It is public knowledge that Muslim troops on the territory of authority of CSB Bijeljina began an attack on April the 1st, 1992." Is that a -- does that reflect what happened at that time? Does that correctly reflect ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partially. The conflict that started was started by the Muslim forces that tried to provoke a clash, and it ended with this armed entrance of Arkan and his forces into Bijeljina. Because the beginning of the war in Bijeljina was such that there was a group of Muslims in front of the Istanbul Cafe and this group set off towards the Serbia Cafe. They were carrying weapons, hand-grenades, et cetera, and they wanted to clash with them. At that time, checkpoints had already been set up around the town and there were members of the Muslim forces there. As to whether that was to mount a defence or to take control of the area, well, this is a subject that could be debated. But there was information according to which it was the Muslim forces that started the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 144 of your statement -- I'm sorry. May I have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have the next item, a 31 July information, be marked and given the next number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in your statement in paragraphs 141 through 147, you describe the operation in Zvornik and the fact that it was basically a success. You arrested a large number of individuals and recovered a lot of property. Could you take a look at that exhibit that's just been given to you and tell us what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a report on what was done in Zvornik. A group of individuals was arrested there, a group of individuals under the command of Zuco, and a lot of vehicles and goods were seized.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a group whose intention was just to engage in looting in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They had two kilos of gold and jewellery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'm reminded by the translators that sometimes you speak too quickly or sometimes don't enunciate clearly enough for them. Would you please keep that in mind. This document appears to be from the MUP of Republika Srpska, giving information about the end of your operation. In your statement, you indicate that this was -- this was a matter of some widespread publicity in that there were international and domestic journalists came to report about it. I see there's no mention of your special unit in the MUP information. Do you know why that would be?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At the bottom it says: "The security situation in Zvornik is more favourable than during the previous days in respect of the measures planned and one can expect the situation to be further stabilised." That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in any of the press announcements or interviews with the journalists after this operation occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When these individuals were brought in in Bijeljina, when they were taken into custody, on the following day, in the premises of the MUP, a press conference was held at which there were about 100 journalists. Half of them were from abroad. On that day, a delegation had arrived from the international press centre in Belgrade. There was a group of journalists, two buses, and they asked for more detailed information about the paramilitary formations. And it just so happened that I had to attend the press conference and I told them what the service had done and I also told them about the number of individuals arrested. I took those journalists out into the yard and showed them these individuals all lined up. They had been taken out from 11 detention cells, and I had lined them up so that the journalists could put questions to them about the circumstances under which they had been taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened with these -- all these men you arrested in Zvornik at that time? How -- how were they dealt with? How were they processed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For those people where we felt they had committed some crimes - and I mean Zuco and his brother - I think there was a journalist from the Duga magazine there, and so other people who were members of that leading structure -- well, there was a criminal report filed and all the documents were submitted and the prosecutor's offices in Bijeljina were informed, and they were kept in custody, whereas other people who were involved in those paramilitary formations were made available to the military authorities and -- in other words, it was in order to avoid them being into any paramilitary units and they had to become incorporated into the official Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska and then the armed forces would deploy units and assign tasks to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question is -- is a more general one: In terms of where they went after they were taken into custody, what happened to those men? Were they taken somewhere from Zvornik by -- by the police or by those of you who arrested them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police put them on buses, and they were taken directly to the Drina division and they were made available to the commander of that division. I can't remember who he was at the time, because I did not go along. There was an armed escort, and so the police took them on those buses and they had lists and everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they -- were they questioned or interviewed in the process?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of proceedings, we interviewed all of them and obtained information that they had. As to those who had more information, we took detailed statements from them and we did not bother with others. We just had a brief talk with them and then they were released. There are quite a few statements on record. I can't remember the exact numbers, but we actually documented everything that took place at Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to have the next item marked as an exhibit. Perhaps this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a good time for a break, but not until after I've given Ms. Loukas an opportunity to address us, because there was an issue you'd like to briefly raise, but I take it not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I'm happy to do that at the beginning of the next session because there's just a detail I wanted to check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have -- you have to check something?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I will make one short announcement. It's the following: The dossiers have been filed and the Chamber had indicated that if within seven days of filing there would be no objection, that they would be admitted. This is to announce to the Defence that the Chamber has asked further information about the dossiers in respect of Kotor Varos and Vogosca, so that you're aware that -- just to clarify the issue, Ms. Loukas, the one is about more than one document found under one tab and the other one is about the number where good cause should be shown if you go beyond the numbers set by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that, Your Honour. And I can indicate your assistant conveyed that information thoughtfully to me just shortly prior -- prior to Your Honours coming on to the bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. But I think if the Chamber asks for further information to the Prosecution, the Defence should be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. And I'm most pleased to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until ten past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you'd like to address us.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two short matters, just quickly. Firstly, there's a witness that's scheduled June 27, 28. I won't mention the name, but the -- only the KRAJ number, 648. In relation to that, there's records of interview or what have you, and they are only in English. I spoke with Mr. Tieger for the Prosecution during the break and -- and, of course, the situation being that Mr. Krajisnik would like the opportunity to read it, as it doesn't exist in B/C/S. And we tried to come to some sort of arrangement whereby this could occur. And, of course, it's -- it's -- it's critical that Mr. Krajisnik also have an opportunity to read this particular document in -- in B/C/S. We tried to come to some sort of arrangement whereby the Prosecution would try to translate half and I could see what could be done with the CLSS in that way. I made some inquiries, and it was indicated to me that in view of the fact that it would not necessarily be an exhibit, that they did not feel that it would fall within their purview. They -- the message that I received appeared to indicate that there may be something I can do with the registry in that regard. And I've tried to call the -- the registry to see if we can do something about it. But, of course, clearly, in terms of the proceedings and the rights of the accused, where there is a document in English and it is to be referred to by the Prosecution and not necessarily become an exhibit, it is something that Mr. Krajisnik should have the opportunity to read in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any audio available from that interview? I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm told that there is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But nevertheless, of course, audio, Your Honour, has problems of its own, because to listen to something takes a lot longer than to read something. And we're dealing with something that is about 270 pages. So to -- to listen to something on an audio, as opposed to being in a position to read something and also highlight it as it were and be able to refer to it, that's another question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're encouraged to continue to seek for a solution of that. Although, if a statement is not to become an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, it may or may not. It -- who knows at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If it becomes an exhibit, it's quite clear it should be -- it should be there in translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, however, under the, I would say, standing case law, the OTP does not have to produce a translation if an audio is there. But if there are specific portions -- and Ms. Loukas, perhaps you could also look at the English to see whether there are certain areas which are of more importance than others and perhaps try to find a mixed solution where you say, "Well, based on our preliminary selection, these and these portions are such that we'd prefer to -- Mr. Krajisnik read them in B/C/S as well as -- not just listening to the audio," and then perhaps some parts that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, nevertheless, Mr. Krajisnik himself has expressed the wish to be able to read the document in its -- in its entirety. And I think that's not an unreasonable wish, in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, all this case law developed upon the existence of a wish to read. I think that's as such clear enough to tell you that the mere wish of Mr. Krajisnik, of course, could not be the answer to the case law. But let's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, we cannot resolve the matter at this very moment in court. We'll further look into the matter, and everyone is encouraged to see whether any solution could be found.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that's what Mr. Tieger and I have been attempting to do, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- find a solution to this issue, and hopefully we can come to a solution that satisfies the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- rights of the accused and the wishes that would make it in fact more efficient and effective to ensure that the -- the material is covered. The second point I wanted to go to, Your Honour, was this: As Your Honours are aware, I've been dealing with the most -- I finished cross-examining the expert, Mr. Nielsen, earlier this week. I'm currently dealing with -- with this witness. Lead counsel has indicated that he wishes me or directs me to also undertake the third witness, who directly follows this witness. In the circumstances, Your Honour, I'm just wondering if I could ensure that there is some break between the end of this witness's evidence and the beginning of the next. I'm wondering if, in terms of the negotiation of the schedule -- and I've attempted to have a preliminary discussion about this with the Prosecution. I'm just wondering if the witness that is to follow could, in fact, follow Mr. Stewart's next witness. I'm not sure if he's protected or not, so I won't mention his name. But that's 677 that I'm talking about. So, Your Honour, that would give me an adequate opportunity to ensure that I have an opportunity to read the material. Because quite frankly, I'm going to need all weekend for this witness. And I -- it's not -- in terms of the time available, it's not conceivable that I could also deal with the one there following, unless we could interpose 677, deal with his evidence, and then I could deal with that witness. Because I'm also doing the other witness after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to come to a schedule that can ensure that I can perform my duties as a Defence counsel effectively in relation to each witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's as such full understanding for you -- for the wish you expressed, Ms. Loukas. Of course, the problem is not whether once a certain interval would be granted but, of course, the issue is whether that's incidental or whether that would happen all the time and --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, you -- of course you are aware of the scheduling order issued by this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And scheduling within those limits, the Chamber accepts a lot in respect of what is agreed between the parties. But if it would in any way put in danger the scheduling order, then the Chamber would have a close look at it and carefully look at whether it's really necessary or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think that this is something that can perhaps be negotiated in such a way that there -- there's no need to waste any court days, as it were, but that also ensures that the Defence has an adequate opportunity to prepare each witness properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber expects further information from the parties on whether they could work on a schedule that would fit within the scheduling order.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the witness may be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Hannis, could you give us any indication on how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to need the rest of the session and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That would certainly also meet Ms. Loukas's wishes not to start cross-examination this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I may find out that I'm not done at 2.15, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll address you at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the one hand, I'm aware that the Chamber has put a lot of questions to the witness as well. That certainly has taken some time. But in view of your 89(F) estimate, I would say that if we take that estimate as a start, add the time taken by the Judges, that we'd be approximately finished by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, we were still talking about Zvornik and the arrest of the Yellow Wasps and those related persons. I want to show you the next item, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could give it an exhibit number. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- consists of a cover letter, a report, and some attached statements or interviews relating to this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described for us the process of how the arrested men were questioned. For the moment, could you just look at the cover page and tell me if you recognise the name at the bottom of that document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Goran Macar, who at the time was in charge of fighting crime within MUP of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if you could look at the next page, which is described as "Information on MUP activities on exposing the criminal activity of Yellow Wasps in Zvornik." Had you seen that document before you came here to prepare for testifying?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a few days ago you showed it to me, but I had never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you recall having read it and -- and can you tell us if it was generally an accurate description of what you had learned in the course of carrying out this operation and arresting these Yellow Wasps.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a whole, it described what we did, but only the basics were included there, not the details referring to the entire operation and the way in which it was carried out. There is reference here to the fact that certain amounts of money, then vehicles and gold that had been taken, that was the case. It does not say here who did it and how come. I don't know whether you need me to say anything else. I mean, to pinpoint the most essential bits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's -- that's all I wanted to ask you about that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to indicate to the Judges and to the Defence counsel that with this report, in it itself it says are attached 65 statements. We have something like -- in the order of 17 statements attached, because those are the only ones we have translated at this point. I anticipate that we may be trying to complete those translations, disclose them to the Defence, and offer them at a later time. Witness 682, who was one of the newest witnesses added, is able to speak to this issue, and we would propose at that time or perhaps in the Zvornik municipality binder to include those additional statements upon translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, you keep in mind what the 23rd, 24th, 35th statement brings new to the previous ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this operation in Zvornik, what happened to the -- the leaders, Zuco and the journalist that you mentioned -- the leaders of this group? Were they -- were they prosecuted at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We prepared the documents and submitted a criminal report to the military prosecutor in Bijeljina, so they were meant to be detained, but as soon as we withdrew from that area, all proceedings were suspended and they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could the next item be given the next exhibit number and shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 28th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would have a question for you, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Yes, I do apologise for interrupting the flow of events.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the witness says: [In English]: "All proceedings were suspended and they were released," [Interpretation] I can see what you mean, but how do you know that? And secondly, who suspended those proceedings? What authority made the decision? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, this next document will speak to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, in that case, I do apologise. So it was a useless question, but I couldn't have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, you anticipated me well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in light of that question from Judge Hanoteau, could you take a look at the document you've just been shown and tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision about releasing this group from custody. It was Zuco, his brother Repic, and other people who had been taken into custody. And the decision came from the court at Bijeljina, and the judge was called Biljana, who was the investigating magistrate of that court. And since the prosecutor did not ask for any proceedings to be instituted against them, that's why they were released from custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that among the leaders of this group, one man was a journalist. Can you tell us from those names which one of those was the journalist, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Milan Timotic, who introduced himself as simply from Duga, from Belgrade. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this document, this indicates that the allegations against these men were that they commandeered passenger vehicles and documents, objects and values -- valuables all of a value exceeding 5.000 dinars. There doesn't appear to be a reference to any other kind of criminal activity. Based on your information in and your investigation and the report you wrote and -- referring it for prosecution, were there any other crimes that these men were alleged to have been involved in, or was it only the theft?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not take any other data except for that theft and robbery. That was what we were looking into. But we did know that prior to those thefts and robbery they had also been committing murders. I'm not talking about mass murder, but they did murder a group of civilians at Celopek, and I got that report from MUP in Zvornik. And they were also identified in that report as people who are prone to killing and would not stop at anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move now to events after the Zvornik operation. You were based in Belgrade, but your home was still in Bijeljina. How often were you returning to your home in 1992, to your home in Bijeljina? I know you mentioned one weekend. How frequently did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever it was possible, I would go home, normally on weekends, Saturdays and Sundays. But if I was busy on the weekends, sometimes I went during the week, because I had my wife and children and my parents there. So any time off I had, I would just go to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In -- in paragraphs 149 to 165 of your statement, you describe in -- in some detail how the local SDS Crisis Staff planned and carried out ethnic cleansing in Bijeljina. And you say in your statement: "This plan was discussed in front of me." Could you give us some details about that. First of all, where did that occur, that the plan for ethnic cleansing in Bijeljina was discussed in front of you? Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the town hall at the office of the Executive Council president, Mr. Kojic, Savo Kojic, who was the president of the Executive Committee, and he was present at that -- in the course of those talks and the president of the Assembly at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately when that was? A month, if you don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not at the very beginning when I came to Bijeljina with the unit. Perhaps -- well, it was between five and ten days later. And the reason why I went to the town hall was their request for me to stop protecting Muslims and to stop interfering with their policies. What I mean is at the time travel documents were being still issued at Bijeljina, and there were calls for Muslims to be issued with those documents in order for them to leave. And they were outraged and they said that my arrival had put a stop to all that and that I was protecting Muslims. And they started telling me about history, and they wanted to -- what was I doing and did I know who Semberija belonged to and who gave me the right to oppose that. And I was criticised for protecting them and I was asked, you know, why had I come there in the first place. And that was the first time I heard, when he mentioned at the first Assembly meeting, he said that the decision would be made for all Muslims to be taken into military units, to become conscripts, and for those who refused to be sacked and for electricity and water -- and telephone lines to be switched off, and whoever opposed it could be referred to the so-called collection centre at Batkovic, which was being set up in the area of a former co-operative farm, Semberija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph 150 that -- that Mauzer and Kojic and Nikic did most of the talking at this meeting. Do you remember who else, if anyone, was present besides those three and yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Vojinovic, was there, and Cican Simic, and I think the secretary of the Municipal Assembly was there. I'm not really certain about that, so do take it with a grain of salt. I think his name was Vojinovic, something like that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say in that paragraph that certain members of the local SDS and the Crisis Staff compiled lists of names of Muslims for cleansing, and you say that you saw a list of names that were held by Moco Stankovic. Can you tell us the circumstances under which you saw that list. When and where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Moco Stankovic and Professor Petrovic and most of them who were more or less active members of SDS. Mr. Moco Stankovic was the president of the local SDS in Bijeljina, and as such he had the authority to draw up a list of people who should be expelled and he compiled that list and through Mauzer and through the Security Services it was done in that way. I must provide you with another detail. When I left Bijeljina, when I went back to Belgrade, I intervened with Moco Stankovic on a number of occasions and asked him to take some people off that list and protect them. To a considerable extent, he complied, I must say. Some people did get taken off the list, and for others he refused, in spite of the fact that I asked him to protect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for one clarification. Did I understand well that the president of the Municipal Assembly was called Mr. Vojinovic and that his secretary was called Mr. -- let me just see. Vojinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Vujic. I was a bit confused about names so similar. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph 151 that Drago Vukovic and Predrag Jesuric were placed in charge of the first phase of this plan. Who was Drago Vukovic? You mention him as a -- as a member of either the local SDS or the Crisis Staff. What was his position in town?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago was a member of the Crisis Staff, but his position was chief of the State Security Service, the secret police service of the Republika Srpska. He was the head of that department in Bijeljina for Central Bosnia. So Drago Vukovic, I knew him from before. He had worked before at the republican MUP, and then just before the war, he left that MUP and so he worked as a journalist at TV Sarajevo up until the war, and after the war he came to Bijeljina because his wife was from Bijeljina, and he joined the SDS and was with them from day one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you -- you told us at one point in time about a man named Vojkan Djurkovic, who was involved in some of this activity of moving Muslims out of Bijeljina. In paragraph 158, you talk about a -- a particular incident where you had contact with him and he showed you a document authorising him to carry out the work of humanitarian resettlement of the Muslim population. From -- and you say you actually saw that document. From what agency or person did that document come?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I must say that I had that conflict with Djurkovic only after I had left Bijeljina with my unit. That was one weekend when I came to Bijeljina. I cycled to town -- or rather, I went to a certain place. And when Djurkovic saw me, he stopped me and he started asking me who I was -- who I thought I was, why I was trying to prevent them from doing what they were doing. He said he was the only person who had the authority to do what he was doing. And there was a tense situation when he said, "Who authorised you to act in such a way?" And then he showed me this document, and it said that Djurkovic from Bijeljina had been authorised to resettle people in a humane way and it said that he shouldn't be obstructed, and it said the president of the Assembly, in the heading of the document, and there was Krajisnik's signature. After that incident, I regretted having not confronted him, having taken him away. He was the sort of person who was cowardly. And that same day I saw Mico Mandic [phoen] and asked him why they were taking people, what they were doing. He said, "I can't confront that. I'm familiar with that very same document," and he said that he had heard -- he said that Mr. Krajisnik had been told about this and Krajisnik replied that he should not meddle. That's all I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a translation -- it's a translation issue, Mr. Davidovic. In your statement, at paragraph 158, I know you say and the other person that you know of who saw this document was Dragoljub Micic, the representative in the National Assembly from Bijeljina. In the transcript it shows up as "Mico Mandic." Can you tell us what's correct. I think perhaps the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Micic. He was a representative from the republic. It wasn't Mandic. That's a mistake. It was Micic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later -- when the Presiding Judge put a question to me and asked me who Djurkovic was, there is one explanation I failed to provide, and I think it's important. Djurkovic is someone who was trained in Erdut and he participated in the fighting in the Croatian battlefield with Arkan. And when a headquarters was established in Badovinci, where is where there was a training ground at the border between Serbia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Djurkovic was one of Arkan's instructors in the camp where he trained members of the volunteer units who went there. I do apologise, but I thought it would be important to point this out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I want to ask you another question about him. In paragraph 165, you mention that Djurkovic told you that he was paid well for this job that he was doing. What did he say about the money he was getting in connection with the humanitarian resettlement of population?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, he made certain claims. I had frequent contact with him because of the people he was taking away. And he said that this was to his benefit, and not only to his benefit. He said that there was a lot of money involved and that I shouldn't meddle in the matter. He said that it was to his advantage and to the advantage of others who made all of this possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say who the others were or who else was benefitting from the money that was being made?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he would share this money with Arkan and some of the money would be taken to the headquarters in Pale, to Krajisnik and Karadzic. Sometimes he would personally deliver the money. He even said that he delivered the money in a plastic bag on one occasion. And he didn't only tell me about this. He told others about this business. And he said that he would sometimes send money through Luka Karadzic, through Momcilo's brother, and in that way he facilitated the delivery of this money. A number of people told me that when Vojkan would go to Pale and when someone from Bijeljina was there, he could then go to see the President. He could see Karadzic and Krajisnik without having announced himself. And this pointed to the fact that what he was doing was done having obtained authorisation from them, and they were fully aware of -- of what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, next I would like to play a video. If we could give that a number and hand around the transcript. I don't know what our numbering process is for videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape will be P782. The transcript will be 782A. The translation of the transcript will be P782A.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And as soon as everyone has a copy of the transcript, we'll play that. It's about a three-minute segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: BBC Correspondent: He was one of the 60 fighters who seized the town of the Serbs at the beginning of the war. Vojkan was especially proud of his expensive Italian sunglasses. Men like him are doing very well these days in the Bosnian Serb republic. At his office, Vojkan had assembled some of the last Muslims ... in population. That means he's in charge of ethnic cleansing. A report prepared for the UN says he's led groups of armed men who have been terrorising the Muslim community. Vojkan cheerfully denies it all. Vojkan Djurkovic: [No interpretation] BBC Correspondent: He's turned ethnic cleansing into an official procedure and turned Bijeljina into such an ethnically Serbian town that these Muslims are desperate to get out. Vojkan Djurkovic: [No interpretation] BBC Correspondent: When permission came through for them to leave, Vojkan made sure we were there. Vojkan Djurkovic: [No interpretation] BBC Correspondent: He gave them time to say their good-byes and to pack up the few possessions that hadn't been stolen. Deportations are no longer done at gunpoint. But Serbs like Vojkan are no less determined to remove Muslims from their towns. It's still ethnic cleansing. The bus dropped them near the front line. They had to walk the last few hundred yards across no man's land. Bosnian government soldiers were expecting them. Vojkan Djurkovic insists he's doing these people a favour. He calls himself a social worker. He believes he'll soon be offered the Nobel Prize for Peace. Vojkan Djurkovic: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Near the end, Mr. Djurkovic is seen to say -- he was talking about they were tourists and going to Berlin and they were free to return. To your knowledge, at that time in Bijeljina were they free to return?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All those who left and didn't return until after the Dayton Agreement had been signed and peace had been established, then some of these people returned. But at the time, no one would have even thought of returning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all I have about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, of course we have a problem because there's no French transcript of certain parts of this video. The parts that were spoken in B/C/S and were translated on our screens in English were not read out and therefore not translated into French. So we have a problem there. We'll consider how to resolve that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry. I hadn't -- I hadn't realised that Your Honour hadn't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the possibilities would be to file a French translation of the transcript or to have it replayed and then to have the English translation as it appears on the screen and in the transcript, that it's spoken out loudly and then translated into French. But at this moment we have an incomplete transcript, especially in the French language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, you saw it was about three -- three and a half minutes. I don't know what the Court's preference is in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's a bit difficult. In this courtroom, some 25 people are kept busy every minute, so three minutes is 25 times three makes 75. I do not know how much time it takes to have this -- this exhibit translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that makes more sense. We'll be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll -- I leave it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I can provide that Monday perhaps -- well, I don't want to commit my language assistant to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, especially not over the weekend, I take it, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a matter of great urgency, but it's a matter of the completeness of the transcript of the trial, which at this moment seems not to hinder any of the parties to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, that's -- that's fine, Your Honour. The only point I would make in respect of this specific video, of course, it's quite clear that what we have is a great deal of commentary from the journalist himself. And I take it the Prosecution are not in fact putting forward all the commentary and nor could they in the circumstances. And it seems to me that -- and quite frankly, I'd be objecting to -- to the commentary overall. It just seems to me the Prosecution is asking for that bit of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel speak into the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I've moved away from the microphone. That bit of commentary right at the end about they're free to return, it seems to me that's the only portion that the Prosecution are seeking of the commentary there from the journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't commentary from the journalist. That was -- those were the words of Mr. Djurkovic. I am seeking the words of Mr. Djurkovic. As far as commentary of the journalist in terms of his conclusion about whether this is ethnic cleansing or not, I'm not proposing that as part of our evidence, Your Honour. That's not -- that's -- that's for you to decide based on everything you hear, and what a BBC correspondent isn't the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the correspondent says that he was one of the 60 fighters, then of course we would not on the basis of that statement establish that there were 60 fighters. On the other hand, sometimes it is important to see whether -- whether any journalists contradict what appears from the other evidence, which might make you more cautious. So to that extent, Ms. Loukas, I think we do agree that this is not the way to establish facts. At the same time, you could not say that it never could have any relevance to look at it, especially if the -- if the reporters at that time came with a totally different story. That's not to say that that story is true but at least to establish that there were two different stories around.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I'm not approaching it from that angle. But it just seems to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's clear that we will not on the basis of an unknown voice-over establish facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, the video we just watched, is the person shown in that video as Vojkan Djurkovic the same Vojkan Djurkovic that you've been talking about having dealings with in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, in the remaining time, I want to go forward and -- and ask you about something that happened when you were working at the federal SUP after all your experiences in 1992, when you were working in state security. In approximately May of 1993, when there was an Assembly session in connection with the proposed Vance-Owen Peace Plan, do you recall having been involved in the security that was provided to the dignitaries attending that session, the foreign dignitaries, including Mr. Milosevic, the head of the Greek government, and the RS officials?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before you put certain other questions to me, you've said that I later started working for the state security. I did not in fact do that. I was in the public security service. I performed the same duties. I still had a uniform, and I performed the duties that I used to perform in the Federal Secretariat. I had to escort dignitaries, federal civil servants, representatives from other countries, and that is what the federal MUP was involved in. So among other things, I had to escort these representatives from other countries, from the United Nations, and these were the regular duties that we had to perform. Similarly, I -- when it comes to Mr. Mitsotakis, the prime minister of Greece, who came to visit Serbia -- or rather, Yugoslavia, on that morning he continued to Bosnia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then the question was how the prime minister of Greece could go to Bosnia-Herzegovina without the agreement of the federal authorities. There was a dilemma, and finally he went to part of Republika Srpska, to Pale, to attend the adoption of the Vance-Owen Plan. And I was responsible for his visit and for escorting him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. In connection with your duties on that occasion, did you have a chance to stand in during a meeting of the SDS Deputies Club?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to any leading whatsoever on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, of course, a question always leads to the extent that it makes clear that what kind of information you are seeking. Mr. Hannis, I do understand the sensitivity of the issue. Could you please see whether you can formulate your questions in such a way that they are not leading in any unacceptable way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I'm unclear on this. I was just trying to ask him yes or no, did he have occasion to be present at a particular event. If he did, then I will ask him what happened. If he wasn't, then that's the end of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that Ms. Loukas even has a problem with the kind of event you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, you couldn't ask a witness: Have you ever been present at an event, Ms. Loukas. So to that extent, you should direct the attention of the witness to something that you'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I invited Mr. Hannis to do it in such a way not unacceptably leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try it this way, Your Honour. I'll try this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 184, you say there was an Assembly session held and that there was a meeting at 10.00 p.m. At this meeting, you were wearing your uniform as a security officer, and you say it appeared that there were two camps, Dodik and the non-SDS deputies on the one hand and the SDS deputies on the other. What happened around midnight that night? Were you present from 10.00 p.m. on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would first have to say or tell you about what happened earlier on so that I later arrived at the meeting that was held at night. I think it's important for me to tell you how it is and that I attended that meeting, and then I will be able to answer the second part of your question. If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could do that very briefly, because the question was what happened at midnight. But if there's any need to have a short introduction, but keep it please short. We are under some time restraints, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went there with a group of people who were responsible for the reception of Mitsotakis and Cosic, who was the president of Yugoslavia at the time. And the chief of protocol and the chief of security for providing escorts were present at a meeting attended by Karadzic, Krajisnik, the Minister of Internal Affairs at the time, who was Hadzic, and I think that there was another person present whom I didn't know. And we informed them in detail about the arrival of Mitsotakis, Cosic and the others, and we informed them about protocol details that would be relevant on the following day. That was the purpose of my presence. And as for the security issues I was involved in later -- well, I spent that night in Pale and a group of people that had come with me returned to Belgrade that night. And when I stayed there, it was possible for me to communicate with representatives who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What at this moment are you talking about? Mr. -- are you talking about the Greek minister or are you -- it's not entirely clear to me. Mr. Hannis has drawn your attention to paragraph 184 of the transcript from -- from the transcript of the -- which is about an Assembly session to be held at Hotel Bistrica on Mount Jahorina and deputies and journalists had gathered there for a 10.00 p.m. meeting, 10.00 at night. And you said: "While attending this meeting, I wore the uniform of a security officer and I was able to get -- to go to any location because of my status. I knew 90 per cent of the assembled deputies. It was apparent that there were two camps, Dodik and the non-SDS deputies on the one hand and the SDS deputies on the other." When you described that situation, Mr. Hannis would like to know what happened on that same day at midnight. So that's two hours later from what you describe in 184.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At about midnight, the representatives of the representative club of the SDS called me. They functioned independently. They were independent of all the other parties that were in the Assembly at the time. I am thinking of the Movement for Yugoslavia above all; Dodik and some others were members of that party. But the club -- there was a club of representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party. I think Vojin Maksimovic was the president of the club and he had called that Assembly, or rather, he had asked for a meeting to be held and Mr. Krajisnik attended it. They were preparing for the Assembly session to be held on the following day, when representatives from Greece and Yugoslavia arrived. And they started make serious preparations for the meeting to be held the following day, and they also indicated that on the following day there could be certain doubts as to whether to accept or reject the Vance-Owen Plan. Krajisnik didn't want the Vance-Owen Plan to be accepted. He wanted the Assembly to reject this plan. He also said that in the course of the Assembly session we had to see how the representatives -- or the deputies from the SDS would act. He said we had to pay much attention to this. And he said that Milosevic could be very convincing and that when he appeared, he could influence the deputies at such an Assembly session and this would be very unfavourable for Republika Srpska. He said it would be very disadvantageous and that one should resist his attempts to influence us. They also said that after Milosevic had taken the floor, someone should take the floor to attack Milosevic, to oppose Milosevic and to oppose his support for the plan and prevent other individuals from supporting his position. And then certain deputies, who were well known for their fiery rhetoric, were called. I think Mr. Vjestica, one of the deputies from the Bihac area, was supposed to take the floor to attack the proposed plan and to contest it. It was also said that if there was a discussion in favour of accepting the plan, he would then give the floor to the deputies who weren't accepting the plan. There might be deputies who would accept the plan, but they would then give the floor to representatives from the Serbian Democratic Party, who would be very fiery when expressing their position -- positions and would try to prevent this plan from being adopted. I must admit that I was unpleasantly surprised by these preparations, and I took certain other measures that I could inform you about if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's described in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's timing, Mr. Hannis, which is -- it's among the best. Mr. Davidovic, we will adjourn for the day, and we'll resume after the weekend. Madam Registrar, I think we start at 9.00 in the morning next Monday. We'd like to see you back not necessarily in this courtroom, I think. Madam Registrar, would it be Courtroom III or Courtroom II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me when I will have completed my testimony? I was informed that today should have been the last day of my testimony. Then it -- now it's been extended until Monday. Will my testimony continue on Tuesday too? I would like to have a rough idea of when my testimony might be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an answer, Ms. Loukas, I'm turning to you but at the same time I'm aware that you have to finish your preparations for the -- for this witness over the weekend. Could you give us any idea?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I would have thought -- at this stage, I can indicate that I would be most of Monday -- most, if not all, of Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Davidovic, I do understand that you're surprised, although it does not surprise me completely that we did not finish this week. We'll try to finish Monday. That would mean that by Monday 2.00 your testimony would be concluded. But I cannot exclude that it takes still some time Tuesday morning. Is that something that causes you great problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Since I'm already here, well, then, I have to stay. There's no other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you at least for your cooperative attitude in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone - no one - about your testimony already given or still to be given. We'll adjourn until next Monday, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
